Title: Hackers help themselves to 1Password's source code and customer data
Context: "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said
Full Text: 1Password is reassuring customers that their vaults remain secure after an attacker breached its systems and stole account information and private source code. The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information. 1Password, which began investigating the intrusion on November 19, hasn't said how many customers were affected, but confirmed that the stolen data includes names and email addresses used to sign in to the service, account identifiers, timestamps showing when users created and last accessed their accounts, and various pieces of non-secret account metadata. The company insists the information that customers actually pay it to protect was beyond the intruder's reach. "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said. Arguably more troubling is the revelation that the intruder gained access to 1Password's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which houses credentials used to keep its products running. The company says it has rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials and that neither its apps nor its browser extensions were affected. 1Password hasn't explained how access to an employee's GitHub account enabled the attacker to deploy malicious code to its backend services, nor has it detailed the extent of the attacker's access to its software build and distribution infrastructure. The company did not respond to The Register's questions. The miscreant also got their hands on tokens embedded in emails sent to some customers as part of account invitations, provisioning, and recovery processes. These tokens aren't enough to access an account on their own, according to 1Password, as users must also authenticate via single sign-on or enter a verification code sent to their registered email address. The company says it specifically notified the small number of users with affected provisioning or recovery processes underway. It found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed provisioning tokens. Still, the breach has prompted the password management biz to beef up those verification codes, replacing the six-digit numeric variety with ten-character alphanumeric codes to make brute-forcing them considerably more difficult. 1Password has booted the intruder out of its GitHub environment, revoked the stolen token, and rolled back the affected backend services to clean versions of the code. It's since shored up security around its development infrastructure and employees' devices, and brought in outside security specialists to review its handiwork. The incident recalls the first stage of LastPass's 2022 breach, when an attacker compromised its development environment and stole source code. Information obtained in that intrusion helped enable a second attack that exposed customer vault backups, including encrypted passwords. The UK Information Commission's Office slapped LastPass with a £1.2 million ($1.6 million) fine last December over the incident, which compromised the personal information of up to 1.6 million UK users. Among the regulator's gripes was that LastPass had fallen short of the higher standard of security expected of a company entrusted with people's passwords. Customers aren't being asked to change their account passwords or Secret Keys, neither of which 1Password stores, although the company is warning users to be on the lookout for phishing attempts. A list of email addresses belonging to people known to use a particular password manager is a handy thing for a phisher to have, especially when said password manager has just given them a plausible pretext for getting in touch. ®

Title: 1Password Hacked, Customer Data and Source Code Stolen in GitHub Account Breach
Context: " "Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers
Full Text:
Popular password management software 1Password on Wednesday disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems that led to the unauthorized access of some customer information, but emphasized that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

"While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including names and email addresses," the Toronto-based company said.

It noted that no customer vault content, including secrets, passwords, and other vault items, account recovery keys, or the keys that secure them, was accessed or compromised as a result of the breach. It also stated that customers do not need to take any action, but cautioned them to stay vigilant against unexpected phishing attempts.

As part of its efforts to remediate the incident, 1Password has disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, hardened GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, restored clean versions of the affected service, and rotated internal credentials. It has also lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

According to the company, the incident dates back to November 19, 2026, when it began investigating suspicious activity after an unknown threat actor gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account.

The attacker is said to have weaponized the account to access source code and push malicious code to its backend services, resulting in the download of administrative data related to its customers, including -

Names

Email addresses

Account and user identifiers, such as account creation and last sign-in times

Public keys

Secure Remote Password protocol parameters

Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery

Non-secret internal metadata about the account, such as version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers

1Password also noted that the tokens embedded in the links cannot be used on their own to gain access to customer accounts, as doing so requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address. However, it noted that a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified.

"The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system," 1Password said. "Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. There is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security."

"Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers."

Title: 1Password Hacked: Customer Names and Emails Copied, Vaults Untouched
Context: “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker
Full Text:
1Password says an attacker stole customer names and emails through an employee’s GitHub account, but vaults and passwords remained safe.

1Password has disclosed that an attacker got into some of its backend systems. The company posted its update on November 25 and says customer vaults weren’t affected. It also says some customer account data was copied.

“An attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including the names and email addresses that customers use to sign into 1Password.” reads the update published by 1Password. “Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected. 1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys.”

An attacker accessed some of company’s backend systems and copied a limited amount of customer data. This affected only some customers and included the names and email addresses they use to sign in. The identity security firm has not said how many customers were affected, a detail also missing from TechCrunch’s report.

The attack started with an employee’s corporate GitHub account. 1Password began investigating on November 19, after detecting signs that someone had accessed the account without permission. The attacker used it to access source code and add malicious code to backend services. These services then downloaded customer-related administrative data. It is still unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s GitHub account.

The copied records include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, and the times each account was created and last signed in. They also hold public keys, which are public by design, and Secure Remote Password parameters, which can’t be used to access an account. The rest is non-secret metadata about 1Password’s internal architecture, such as numeric version and file identifiers.

One item deserves more attention: tokens from emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery. A token only completes the process when it’s paired with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address.

“The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits.” continues the report. “This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.”

Even so, 1Password changed the code format. It now uses ten letters and numbers instead of six digits. This makes it almost impossible for attackers to guess the code by trying different combinations.

Provisioning invitations are used for the SCIM Bridge and Hosted Provisioning services. A small number of users were in the provisioning process during the incident, and 1Password has contacted them directly. The company also says it found no evidence that anyone used the exposed tokens to take over accounts.

The attacker also accessed more than customer records. They copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the CI/CD system, which stores secrets used to run 1Password’s infrastructure. The company says its source code does not contain customer data or user secrets. It has also changed all credentials that may have been exposed.

The company says services, availability and product security weren’t affected. Vaults and the items in them weren’t touched, and neither were the keys that protect them or the account recovery keys. 1Password’s apps and browser extensions weren’t affected either, and it doesn’t store account passwords or Secret Keys.

“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.” states the report.

To mitigate the incident. 1Password disabled the GitHub account, revoked the stolen token and removed the access the attacker created. It restored clean versions of the affected service, rotated or revoked the internal credentials, tightened its GitHub, CI/CD and endpoint controls, and added detections for this kind of attack. It also brought in independent experts to check its containment and remediation.

Several questions remain open; the company hasn’t disclosed how many customers were impacted or whether they’ve all been notified. At this time it is unclear who is behind the athe attacker is, or whether anyone has made demands. The Hacker News also describes the attacker only as unknown.

For customers, 1Password says there’s nothing to update in your account. It does ask you to watch for unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations or account recovery attempts you didn’t start. Phishers read the news too.

Legitimate messages follow a simple rule: only enter your password or Secret Key in the official 1Password app or website. Always open the app yourself or type the website address manually. You only need your Secret Key the first time you sign in on a new device or browser. If someone asks for it at any other time, treat it as suspicious. You can report suspicious messages to support@1password.com.

1Password says it will update its post if it discovers anything new. The company has also published its Security Whitepaper since 2015, giving users more information about how it protects their data.

Title: 1Password Hit by Backend Breach via Hijacked Employee GitHub Account
Context: "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password wrote
Full Text:
Password manager 1Password has suffered a backend breach after an attacker took over a staff member's corporate GitHub account and used it to take customer account data.

The company began investigating on November 19 after detecting signs of the intrusion, it said in an incident post.

"At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password wrote.

From GitHub to Backend Services

With the GitHub account, the attacker reached 1Password's source code and pushed malicious code into backend services, which then pulled administrative records on a subset of users.

Private repository code was also copied, and the attacker got into the company's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) system. 1Password said the source code held no user secrets, but the CI/CD environment contained infrastructure secrets, which it rotated.

Exposed records included customers' names, email addresses, account and user IDs, the dates accounts were created and last signed in, public keys and parameters used by the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol.

Tokens in some invitation, provisioning and recovery emails were also exposed, and those affected, "a small number of users," were told directly. 1Password said a token only worked together with a single sign-on (SSO) login or a code emailed to the account's address.

Read more on GitHub supply chain attacks: New Supply Chain Attack Compromises Tens of Thousands of GitHub Repositories

Vaults Untouched, Codes Lengthened

The keys protecting vaults, account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and its browser extensions were not affected, the company said. It added that it did not store users' account passwords or Secret Keys.

1Password shut down the compromised GitHub account, canceled the token the attacker had stolen and cut off their access. It also rotated or revoked internal credentials that might have been exposed, tightened controls around GitHub, CI/CD and endpoints and introduced new detections.

As a precaution, 1Password lengthened invitation and recovery codes to 10 letters and numbers, up from six digits. It also engaged outside security experts to verify its containment and clean-up work.

The company said customers did not need to change anything in their accounts but should watch for phishing, such as unexpected invitations or recovery requests. Its internal checks found no evidence that exposed provisioning tokens had been used to take over accounts, and the company said it would update its post if anything changed.

Title: 1Password Breach Exposes Customer Data, Internal Source Code
Context: However, the company noted that the exposed tokens cannot be exploited on their own and there is no evidence that the attacker hijacked user accounts
Full Text:
Password management and identity security company 1Password revealed on Wednesday that a hacker stole customer information and proprietary source code. 1Password says customer vaults are not affected.

The company launched an investigation on November 19 after discovering that an employee’s corporate GitHub account may have been compromised.

The attacker used the account to deploy malicious code to backend services and exfiltrate customer records. The compromised customer records include names, email addresses, account identifiers, public cryptographic keys, authentication parameters, account activity times, and non-secret metadata.

In addition, the threat actor obtained source code from private repositories and accessed the company’s CI/CD system, potentially exposing infrastructure credentials.

According to 1Password, the hacker also obtained tokens from emails sent to users for account invitations, provisioning, and recovery.

A “small number” of individuals who were undergoing provisioning or recovery during the intrusion have been notified. However, the company noted that the exposed tokens cannot be exploited on their own and there is no evidence that the attacker hijacked user accounts.

A 1Password representative noted on the company’s community forum that the stolen authentication data included Secure Remote Password verifiers derived from user account passwords and Secret Keys. The verifiers cannot be used directly for authentication, and brute-forcing account passwords would require the associated Secret Keys, which 1Password does not store.

1Password highlighted that customer vaults and the cryptographic keys protecting them were not compromised. “We have no evidence that encrypted vaults were downloaded or accessed,” a 1Password community manager said.

The breach also does not impact client applications, browser extensions, and account recovery keys.

It’s unclear how many users are affected and how the hacker gained initial access to the corporate GitHub account.

In response to the intrusion, 1Password disabled the compromised GitHub account, invalidated a stolen token, replaced potentially compromised infrastructure credentials, and restored clean versions of affected services.

The company said its investigation, conducted with independent cybersecurity experts, is still ongoing. Customers do not need to take any action, but have been advised to watch for phishing attacks that could exploit news of the incident.
